extracted.intended_audience: U.S. Patent Office personnel (examiners) and patent applicants/attorneys (practitioners)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating and weighing rebuttal evidence and arguments offered by applicants to overcome prima facie obviousness rejections under 35 U.S.C. § 103. Covers types of admissible evidence, required nexus and commensurateness, limits on attorney argument, and proper/legal rationales (e.g., obvious-to-try, teaching-away).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of rebuttal arguments and evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Office personnel should consider all rebuttal arguments and evidence presented by applicants; error not to consider evidence presented in the specification or factual evidence submitted to counter a rejection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite Soni, Alton, Beattie, Piasecki. Do not give no weight to evidence except in rare circumstances. Evidence submitted in a timely manner should be considered on the record. If evidence is deemed insufficient to rebut the prima facie case, Office personnel should specifically set forth the facts and reasoning that justify this conclusion (see MPEP § 716 - § 716.10 for additional information).

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of permissible rebuttal evidence / secondary considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Rebuttal evidence may include secondary considerations such as commercial success, long-felt but unsolved needs, failure of others, unexpected improved properties, copying by others, evidence of the state of the art, level of skill in the art, and beliefs of those skilled in the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples and citations: Graham (commercial success, long-felt need), Piasecki (commercial success), Dillon (unexpected properties for compounds), GPAC and Hybritech (copying), Oelrich and Piasecki (expert opinions on level/need). Rebuttal evidence may also show the prior art fails to disclose or render obvious a method for making a claimed compound (see Hoeksema).

rubrics_metrics.name: Unexpected results must be supported by evidence (not argument)
rubrics_metrics.description: A showing of unexpected results must be based on evidence, not attorney argument, conclusory statements, or speculation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comparative data or factual support is required; conclusory statements (e.g., claiming unusually low immune response without comparative data) are insufficient to overcome a prima facie case of obviousness. See Dillon, In re Mayne, and MPEP § 716.02 - § 716.02(g).

rubrics_metrics.name: Nexus requirement between proffered evidence and the claimed invention
rubrics_metrics.description: To be entitled to substantial weight, applicant should establish a nexus between the rebuttal evidence and the claimed invention; objective evidence of nonobviousness must be attributable to the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The PTO relies on the applicant to provide hard evidence of commercial success or other secondary considerations (In re Huang). Evidence of commercial success for articles not covered by the claims is not probative (Paulsen). Applicant bears the burden of establishing nexus; examiners should consider whether evidence is commensurate in scope (Kulling, Grasselli).

rubrics_metrics.name: Commensurateness of evidence in scope with the claimed invention
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence must be reasonably commensurate in scope with the claimed invention; however, applicant need not show unexpected results across the entire claimed range.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence that a compound/composition possesses superior properties in one of a spectrum of common properties can suffice if a skilled artisan could reasonably extend the probative value (Chupp, Clemens). One test may be insufficient where no adequate basis exists to conclude other claimed compounds would behave similarly (Lindner, Grasselli, Greenfield).

rubrics_metrics.name: Weighing and relative weight of rebuttal evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Office personnel must weigh the proffered rebuttal evidence and arguments and determine the appropriate weight to accord each piece of evidence; not all evidence need be accorded the same weight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Considerations include nexus and commensurateness. If the obviousness rejection is maintained, the record should show that evidence of obviousness outweighs evidence of nonobviousness (preponderance of the evidence standard per MPEP § 706). See PharmaStem, Hearing Components, and MPEP § 716.01(d), § 716 for further guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attorney argument does not replace evidence (except admissions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Arguments of counsel are not evidence and cannot take the place of factually supported objective evidence, unless the statement is an admission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See In re Schulze, In re Geisler. Attorney statements must be supported by affidavits or declarations under 37 CFR 1.132 (see MPEP § 716.01(c) for examples). Admissions may be used as evidence per MPEP § 2129 and § 2144.03.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mere recognition of latent properties or additional advantages is insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: Prima facie obviousness is not rebutted merely by recognizing additional advantages or latent properties present but not recognized in the prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discovering an unknown but inherent function in the prior art would not confer patentability (In re Wiseman, Baxter). Recitation of an additional advantage associated with doing what the prior art suggests does not lend patentability to an otherwise unpatentable invention (Lantech). See MPEP § 716.02 - § 716.02(g).

rubrics_metrics.name: Physical combinability is not required; consider combined teachings
rubrics_metrics.description: The test for obviousness is not whether features of a secondary reference may be bodily incorporated into the primary reference but what the combined teachings of the references would have suggested to a person of ordinary skill in the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See In re Keller, In re Sneed, In re Nievelt. However, the claimed combination cannot change the principle of operation of the primary reference or render it inoperable for its intended purpose (see MPEP § 2143.01).

rubrics_metrics.name: Cannot show nonobviousness by attacking references individually when rejections are based on combinations
rubrics_metrics.description: A reply limited to what a subset of applied references teaches or fails to teach, or that fails to address the combined teaching of the applied references, may be treated as attacking references individually and thus be insufficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the applicant's reply addresses both each applied reference's deficiencies and the combined teachings/suggestions, reliance on Keller is not appropriate. See In re Keller and In re Merck & Co. (Mouttet discussion).

rubrics_metrics.name: Number of references combined is not, by itself, evidence against obviousness
rubrics_metrics.description: Reliance on a large number of references in a rejection does not, without more, weigh against a finding of obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The court has upheld rejections based on numerous references (e.g., thirteen references in In re Gorman). Examiners may rely on multiple references where appropriate to the rationale.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not import unclaimed specification limitations into claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Although claims are interpreted in light of the specification, limitations from the specification are not read into the claims if they are not recited in the claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See In re Van Geuns, Constant v. AMD, and related case law. Results or limitations discussed only in the specification may be germane to patentability of an embodiment but not to the claims if not claimed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economic infeasibility does not negate obviousness
rubrics_metrics.description: The fact that a combination would not be made by businessmen for economic reasons does not mean a person of ordinary skill in the art would not make the combination for technical reasons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See In re Farrenkopf: technological compatibility/predictability, not business convenience/cost, governs the obviousness analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nonanalogous art arguments and analogous art guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: Arguments that a reference is nonanalogous should be evaluated under the analogous art principles; see MPEP § 2141.01(a) for applicable case law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whether a reference is analogous affects whether it is properly relied upon in an obviousness rejection; consult MPEP § 2141.01(a).

rubrics_metrics.name: Impermissible hindsight is improper but reconstruction is allowed when based on PHOSITA knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicants may argue that an examiner's obviousness conclusion is based on hindsight; reconstruction based on hindsight is proper only if it takes into account only knowledge within the level of ordinary skill at the time of the invention and does not include knowledge gleaned only from applicant's disclosure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See In re McLaughlin. The absence of an express, written motivation to combine in the prior art is not dispositive (Ruiz). See MPEP § 2141 and § 2143 for guidance regarding prima facie obviousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Age of references is not persuasive absent evidence of tried-and-failed
rubrics_metrics.description: The mere age of references does not, by itself, show unobviousness of their combination unless there is evidence that, notwithstanding knowledge of the references, the art tried and failed to solve the problem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See In re Wright and Ex parte Meyer. Historical gap alone does not preclude reliance on older references.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obvious-to-try rationale: when it supports obviousness
rubrics_metrics.description: An 'obvious to try' rationale may support obviousness where one skilled in the art is choosing from a finite number of identified, predictable solutions with a reasonable expectation of success.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: KSR sets the standard; apply caution where prior art gives no indication of which parameters are critical or where multiple possible choices exist. See KSR, In re O'Farrell, and MPEP § 2141 descriptions of 'obvious to try' errors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lack of suggestion to combine is only one possible rationale
rubrics_metrics.description: A suggestion or motivation to combine references is an appropriate method for determining obviousness but is only one of several valid rationales recognized (e.g., functional approach); lack of explicit suggestion does not automatically negate other rationales.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: KSR identified several rationales consistent with proper determinations of obviousness; see MPEP § 2141 and § 2143 for examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teach-away: nature and weight of teachings against the invention
rubrics_metrics.description: A prior art reference that 'teaches away' from the claimed invention is a significant factor that must be weighed; the nature of the teaching is highly relevant and must be weighed in substance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A mere disclosure of alternatives is not necessarily teaching away (Fulton). If references teach away from their combination, combining them may be improper (Grasselli). See In re Gurley for how a teaching that an alternative is 'inferior' may still not prevent obviousness if the inferior alternative is nonetheless useful for the applicant's purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior art must be enabling to support a conclusion of obviousness for compounds
rubrics_metrics.description: A conclusion of obviousness based on structural relationships between compounds requires that the references relied upon, together with the knowledge of a person skilled in the art, be enabling so as to put the public in possession of the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the prior art fails to disclose or render obvious a method for making a claimed compound at the time the invention was made, this may overcome a presumption of obviousness (Hoeksema, Le Grice, Grose). Applicant may bear the burden of producing evidence that the reference would not enable a skilled artisan to produce the claimed compounds.
